name: Braised Pork Shoulder with Fennel and Tomato

prose.intro_html: Pork shoulder is one of the great bargains in the meat case. It is the cut butchers cannot charge much for because it needs time, and time is free. You brown it, build a quick pan of fennel, onion, garlic, and tomato paste under it, then let the oven do the work while you go do something else. The fennel cooks down soft and sweet and loses its sharp edge, the pork pulls apart with a fork, and the whole thing tastes like it came out of a restaurant kitchen. Built at 14 servings it runs about {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein a serving, with under 12 grams of carbs. That is a slow Sunday braise priced like a weeknight.
shop_smart: Eight and a quarter pounds of pork shoulder is the whole game. This is where nearly all of the money and all of the protein live, and it is still one of the cheapest cuts you can buy because it rewards patience instead of a fancy grade. Reach for a big boneless shoulder, sometimes labeled Boston butt, rather than the small trimmed roasts so you are paying for pork, not packaging.

Five fennel bulbs and a couple of red onions are the vegetable body of the braise. The fennel is the whole point of this dish, so buy the firm bulbs with the fronds still attached and trim them down at home. They cook low and slow into something soft and sweet, and the two and a half red onions melt right in beside them.

Nine and a quarter cups of chicken broth carries the braise. This is the liquid the pork cooks in and the pan juices you spoon over every container, so a couple of the big cartons covers it. Any plain chicken broth works here, so skip the fancy bone broth and buy the everyday one.

Tomato paste, garlic, cider vinegar, mustard, thyme, and olive oil build the flavor. A little tomato paste and a splash of cider vinegar give the braise its backbone, and the garlic, mustard, and thyme round it out. These are pantry and produce staples you buy once and cook with for a long time.
make_it: Weigh your empty Dutch oven or the biggest oven-safe pot you own and write the number down. You will use it at the end to split this into 14 even servings by weight instead of eyeballing every container.

Heat the oven to 375 degrees F. Cut the pork shoulder into large chunks about 3 inches across. Heat the olive oil in the pot over medium-high heat and brown the pork on all sides, working in batches so the pot is not crowded. Move the browned pork to a plate and set it aside.
Quarter the fennel bulbs and thinly slice the red onion. Add both to the same pot and cook gently for a few minutes, stirring now and then, until they start to soften.
Thinly slice the garlic. Stir the garlic, apple cider vinegar, dried thyme, yellow mustard, and tomato paste into the pot and cook one minute more, scraping the browned bits up off the bottom.
Return the pork and any collected juices to the pot. Pour in the chicken broth and bring it up to a boil. Cover the pot and move it to the oven for 1 hour.

Take the pot out, stir, and turn the pork. Return it covered for 30 minutes, then uncovered for 30 minutes more, until the pork is fork-tender and the fennel is soft. If the pan looks dry along the way, top it up with a little extra broth. Shred the pork with two forks and stir it back through the vegetables and pan juices.

Weigh the full pot and subtract the empty weight from Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide by 14 and spoon that exact weight into each container, giving every one an even share of pork, fennel, and juices.
prose.portion_html: Set the full pot on your scale and subtract the empty weight you wrote down in Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide that number by 14 and spoon that exact weight into each container, sharing the pork, fennel, and juices evenly. Every serving lands near {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein.

steps: Weigh the empty pot and write the number down.
Cut the pork into large chunks and brown it in the olive oil, then set it aside.
Soften the quartered fennel and sliced red onion in the same pot.
Stir in the garlic, cider vinegar, thyme, mustard, and tomato paste and cook one minute.
Return the pork, add the chicken broth, bring to a boil, cover, and braise at 375 degrees F.
Braise covered then uncovered until fork-tender, shred the pork, and stir it back through.
Weigh the pot, subtract the empty weight, and divide across 14 containers.
